text:
I AM NOT A LAWYER.  I would suggest that you do the inventory before you meet with your lawyer.

The first thing to note is that it sounds like you may have performed an illegal eviction.  He might be able to sue you for that.  There's not much you can do about that now.  Don't discuss or put into writing any of the history on this.  Limit your conversations in general.

In terms of the property, I'm not sure why this is so difficult to determine.  Google search for `california tenant abandoned property`.  Here's one result from [nolo.com](https://www.nolo.com/legal-encyclopedia/handling-tenants-abandoned-property-california.html).  Here's an excerpt:

- California landlords must follow very specific steps before disposing of the property that is clearly abandoned.  First, you must inventory and store the personal property in a safe location. You can decide to keep the property in the rental unit, but the rental unit must be safe and secure. Then, you must give the tenant notice of the abandoned property **etc. etc. etc. read the rest....**

I want to point you to some items:

- **a statement that reasonable storage costs will be charged to the tenant and the tenant must pay those costs before claiming the property.**  I wouldn't make this retroactive without an ok from the lawyer.  How do you figure this?  You can look at the cost for a storage unit of comparable size, charged by the month. 

- **If you believe the property is worth less than $700, then you don’t have to sell the property. You can either keep it for your own use or dispose of it in any legal manner (see Cal. Code of Civ. Proc. § 1988(a)).** If the total value is less than $700, it makes things a bit easier for you.  I can't tell you to lie, but don't shoot yourself in the foot by overestimating the value of any of his items.  

- **the time frame that the tenant (or owner of the property) has to claim the property** Give him the opportunity to get his stuff during reasonable hours and days. You don't have to be available 24/7 for him. 

There's NO such law that you cannot touch his belongings, that's absurd.  You think that apartment complexes leave junk in their apartments when people leave and abandon their stuff?  Take a video inventory of everything in the garage, then an inventory of everything in the room, then move all non-valuable items from the room to the garage, and make a note of that.  Move all valuable items to a closet. Then follow the standard process for abandoned property.

text:
First, I'm going to answer your questions. Then, I'm going to give you advice. Please bear with me.

> Question: assume I moved overseas...tomorrow? Next week? and moved to a small town in EU? Anywhere. What are the legal consequences of me leaving my child behind, unannounced.

If you're the kid's only form of support and you walk away, then you could easily face extraditable criminal charges, meaning that you may be shipped home by whatever country you move to so that you can face the music. A conviction for child neglect may also make it hard to obtain citizenship or permanent residence in another country for years afterwards.

If you leave your kid in your partner's care, then you are not neglecting them. If you leave your kid in someone else's care, you are still responsible if they fall short.

Moving to another country is not as simple as upping sticks and getting on a plane. You need a visa, which takes time, and generally you need some legal justification for why one should be issued, such as schooling or work, which means you may not be able to start the visa process yet. If you immigrate without a visa, you can be deported if and when the authorities find you.

> I also know that most EU countries offer reciprocal child support enforcement laws that can be enforced upon their residents. How much are these treaties enforced?

Most EU countries actively enforce support child welfare treaties.

> Can he/she go to court and say I abandoned my child without notification and strip me of my rights to see him/her again till my child is 18 years old? 

If you flee to another country and remain there for an extended period (months, at least), then yes, your coparent has a good argument that you abandoned your kid. That may mean you lose your parental rights outright if they and their future partner want to adopt your kid, or that you need to start from zero to re-establish visitation and custody if you ever move back.

> Will I have rights to visitation?

You will have to seek that through the courts where your child lives, and moving out of country without a plan or any communication will count against you. In particular, you can assume that you _cannot_ bring your kid with you out of the country, once you pull a stunt like that: the courts will tend to view you as a very high risk for parental kidnapping.

> Have other's done this? Is there a checklist of steps to take?

It's more common to flee the country to try to avoid child support, and even that's not very effective.

>  I don't know what else to ask, as I have just begun to consider this, but it is starting to seem as my only way out. 

Here's where the _advice_ starts: that's the abuse brain talking. This is a grandiose plan that, superficially, appears to solve your problems, but actually creates more new problems than it actually solves.

**Please contact a local domestic abuse shelter and get out of your ex's home.**

You can move out of your ex's home and bring your kid with you, up to the limits of your current custody decree. Staying in the jurisdiction and making sure your kid is cared for and looked after are good ideas, and will help your case as you seek to amend custody. Even if you opt to leave your kid behind, _you can still leave_ without having to travel to another country.

Domestic abuse groups see people in your state all the time: fear that your partner will keep pursuing you, keep pushing you, and keep abusing you is _normal_. One of the first things a shelter can do is handle your mail, so that you never have to see your ex again even as you sort this out. Many shelters prioritize women, unfortunately, but there are shelters out there for husbands and ex-husbands of abusive wives. Whatever your gender and situation, you can get help.

Once you are out of your ex-partner's sphere of influence, get into intensive personal counselling. Rebuilding your sense of self and your boundaries is as much an appropriate medical intervention after abuse as casting your leg would be if you broke it, and in any case, you deserve the support.

If you already live apart from your ex, then your next step is to restrict all communication to writing, through something recorded and moderated. That could be a PO box you check once a week, or a platform like OurFamilyWizard. Unless your custody orders require it, you never have to speak to your ex or answer the phone, nor do you have to put up with texts, emails, facebook messages, or any other intrusions on your life.

Physically distancing yourself from your ex, and cutting communication down to the narrowest possible channels, also means that it will be much, much harder for them to manufacture legal trouble for you. They can't argue you assaulted them if you haven't been in the same room as them in months, for example, or that you're stalking them if you never visit their home.

I say this because fleeing to another country to avoid this situation simply isn't gonna work. That's not how international travel works, and that's not how your obligations to your kids work. At best, you'll get a brief vacation before you have to confront this situation again, and you'll spend a lot of money in the process with very little to show for it. It's as self-destructive as most other panic plans, and there's absolutely no reason you need to hurt yourself to protect yourself.

I think that it may be of some use to sort of imagine this guy from a sort of third-person view as if though watching him and you talking from an aerial view. There is a reason for this.

It seems that at some point he told you that he deleted, or was going to delete the pictures of his ex. He didn't. He probably didn't "forget", because he probably never had the intent to do delete those pictures. That is because one does not simply keep pictures of a 6 year long relationship. Such pictures are either deeply hated, or deeply treasured, in most occasions.

I am assuming that after he told you that he was going to delete the pictures, he did not only not delete them, but that he actually looked at them. Maybe not right after your conversation, but possibly sometime afterward.

That is why I suggested that you imagine or visualize him speaking to you, then walking away, and then looking at the pictures. So that you could quite literally "get the picture".

It seems to me that you two are not on "equal-grounds" emotinally. People in your situation never are. By that I mean that if two people date, and the first one has feelings for their past half-a-decade long relationship, and the other person actually likes that first person, then the second person will be at a serious emotional disadvantage. You are that second person. If you two ever become angry at each other, you might love/like him enough not to be hurtful, but he might not. In the same way, you are more likely to fall, and note the word fall, in love with him, than he is with you.

Not only that, and not to be sexist or anything, but you are also at an emotional disadvantage since you are a young girl dating an older man.

When you were in kindergarten he was already high school. Age matters. Maybe not in love, age doesn't matter in love, but that isn't love because he is obviously occupied with his own feelings for this other girl.

text:
What a crappy hand you both were dealt! So many dreams and hopes you both have had to grieve. I'm sure this isn't the marriage that either of you had pictured when you said your vows. I know you have so much on your plate, but I hope you both are seeing therapists to work on processing that loss. 

As for whether to stay or leave... No one can know which choice is right except for you. I imagine your choices seem to be "can I ever be happy if I stay?" or "can I live with myself if I do not?" Those are both deeply personal questions that depend a lot on who you are and how you find your joy and create meaning in your life. 

I think the 2 separate but very much tangled together issues here are 1) caregiver fatigue and 2) change in the dynamic of your marriage relationship. 

You mentioned being turned down for SSDI, but not the reason they gave. Have you also applied for SSI? It is also through social security, but has different criteria for approval. Depending on the state you are in you should also contact your local health department and ask for a nursing home screening. An RN should come out to do an assessment to determine skilled nursing needs. Depending on your insurance, some home health care may be covered.  You also mentioned medical bills, depending on your income it may be possible that you could meet a Medicaid "spend down" which might provide some reprieve from expenses, your local Department of Social  Services would be the place to start  with this question. Honestly, I've known couples that have gotten divorced only so the ill spouse would become eligible for Medicaid so they could access the care they need. 

Hopefully, if you can get some services in place to assist it will provide you with the space you need to decide if this marriage is still right for you. And if so, will shift your role to not feel as overwhelmed with caregiving. And if not, will have some supports and resources lined up to provide care for your wife in your absence. 

I know this can't be an easy choice for you.

text:
I am a housing lawyer. u/grasshoppa1 is correct. When you make a maintenance request, the owner or their agent has a reasonable belief that the need for entry is acknowledged by the tenant. They can not enter, say, a month later, nor can they use entry to do work that isnt necessary, but if they are examining or repairing someone the tenant has called to their attention, provided they are entering in a reasonable timeframe, you have no recourse. 

Legally speaking, your right to sold occupancy is called "quiet enjoyment." This term is often confused to mean silence or noise levels, but the term "quiet" in real estate means "without another person on entity with a claim to the title." Since your lease (and state law) require the landlord to give 24 hour notice of nonemergency entry, this applies to any matter that you have not requested -or- is requested but a delayed response. 

Your remedy if the landlord repeatedly enters without notice in non requested, non emergency matters is being allowed to break your lease and move elsewhere. There is no legal process in which you would recover money. The only extant one is you can get an injunction that serves as a court order the landlord must abide by the lease terms. This is pointless and expensive. 

But here, I hate to say it, is you being upset for nothing. If you want them to give notice prior to entry, then make requests for maintenance in writing and request notice of entry prior to doing so. But frankly, any legal action if they do not would almost assuredly be futile.
label: ANECDOTE

text:
Great to see you have an entrepreneurial mindset, but you are trying to solve a minor problem from the wrong direction, man. 

First of all, let me poke an obvious hole in your math. If I can buy brand new furniture for $760, and if it costs $1,200 to hire movers to move it, then if I had to move, I would call Goodwill to pick up my furniture for free and then buy new furniture for another $760. Under no circumstances is it rational for someone to pay more to move something from place to place than it would cost to buy a new version of that thing. 

You are marketing a service to a demographic that doesn't exist. People who are moving nearly every year are almost certainly younger and with less disposable income. These people *do not hire movers*. Paying for convenience isn't a concept because they can't afford it. People who are willing and able to pay for movers likely don't move all that often and have more valuable belongings, meaning that they would prefer *their own belongings*, not rentals.

I also want to address your assertion that it is a generational thing that young people move around so much ... it's not. People 22-30 move around, sure, but as people get older, they naturally settle into careers and living situations that are, in general, more stable. To be clear, though, there is not an entire generation of people who routinely move every 1-2 years as a matter of course. When my friends and I got out of college, most of us moved at least once a year... eight years later, my only friends and family who have moved in the past year have a) moved cities due to job relocation, b) purchased homes or c) gotten married/divorced. It just isn't reasonable to expect that people will use your service, were it to exist, for more than a few years before they are in a stable situation.

When I moved into my apartments in college, I moved myself with my own car since I just bought my furniture from the person who was in the apartment before me, and I sold it to the person who came after me when I left. After college, I moved by borrowing a friend's pickup truck once and using a U-haul twice. Three moves cost a combined $500, and it was only that much because one of the times I dropped off at a different location than I rented the U-haul.

If you want to look to rent furniture, don't look to individuals; look to landlords. You can contract with a landlord, who can offer to furnish an apartment for an added cost. Of course, this service has been around for years, so your entry into the market would be to build a better mouse trap, not create a whole new thing.

I don't trust the calculators either. I'd recommend forecasting your goals and potential larger expenses for the next 0-30 years. Example: Your cars won't last forever - what is the cost of your ideal replacement vehicle every 5-10 years?  More expensive houses generally mean more expensive maintenance... Property tax increases are guaranteed (if you have them)... You child will be more expensive as he/she gets older - do you plan on having another (which would increase child care and other costs)?

I am probably not telling you anything you don't already know but this is how I personally budget these scenarios.

Don't look so much at your expenses now but try to estimate the lifestyle you want to live in the future and budget backwards from that. Those online calculators do not take into account all of those specific details of your financial life (and goals) so I find them useful as a guideline at best.

He went to a 4 year university and got two degrees while he was there (so basically, he did well in school and learned a lot). I don't know how he got the internship exactly- that is, I don't know if he had signed up for something at school or not, but Microsoft reached out to him in the end and he took the internship job for a year then applied for a full time position and got the job. It wasn't exactly what he wanted to do at first, but MS is a huge company and he knew he'd be able to move around in the company after a while and hopefully get into gaming and eventually he did. That is, he first worked on Kinect, and then on Holo-lens. He worked WITH some game devs who worked on Halo and stuff but he's never worked on a game like that. Now he's working with a studio (Against Gravity). They've got some games out for Vive. He's done some other VR work as well, also for Vive. 

I'm sure some people go right from college to a large gaming company but I haven't heard great things from people who have gone that route. I'd get very familiar with subreddits for people interested in software engineering, look for people close to your age who are a few steps in front of you to gather up some info about what you can expect from school and so on. But first thing is school and a lot can change once you're there too. Best thing you can do for yourself if you're not in college yet, is to get ok with studying and focusing on schoolwork and actually learning rather than just sort of skating by. The biggest issue I see with people IN college is that they're treating it like highschool. They're half-assing the work and trying to get a passing grade rather than actually trying to learn the subject matter. If you can teach yourself to learn, you'll be ahead of the game. Lots of people are developers but there are only so many good ones and even fewer great ones. You HAVE to do the work, and you HAVE to be interested in it to be great at it. 

As far as specific step-by-step "how to become a developer" you'll have to talk with a lot of developers and find out what they did, what decisions they made that were good and bad, and how they dealt with failures along the way. Don't just focus on the superstars, or reading about that one guy who spun up a game company and became rich over night- Talk with any software developer you can and get their input on the industry as a whole and gaming specifically. > My lawyer is clearly on friendly terms with the court and the officers and seems to want to please them.

These people spend day in and day out with each other. Of course, they are friendly. With that being said, your lawyer is duty-bound to act in your best interest. If they are recommending pleaing, I would listen to them. No one here is going to disagree with an actual lawyer. 

Also, keep in mind that the prosecution will often settle for far less than they expect to get if the case went to trial, to avoid seeing a million DUI's clogging up the court system. For this reason, I hazard to guess that the plea is probably in your best interest. 

With that being said, the ultimate choice is up to you. If this is the hill you want to die on, that is your right. I suspect the lawyer is suggesting a plea as it'll likely cost you more to fight it (with a lawyer) then the plea.
label: ADVICE

Although you didn’t call, you are still liable for the charges. However, as others have pointed out, the party at faults insurance should cover it fully. To cover yourself, I would call the service and explain the situation. Inform them of the other persons instance information if you have it, and tell them that’s who they can hunt down for the balance. I’ve known some services to receive a call/complaint similar to this and just waive the charge entirely. Good luck to you!
